books.section: The War and the Working Class
American Involvement in Vietnam, World War II–1963

primary_sources: Selective Service System draft calls, 1965 (public record)

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from the grounding books' account of who served in Vietnam

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of who served in Vietnam, from the grounding books.
stimulus.text: Paraphrase of who served in Vietnam. About 80 percent of the troops in Vietnam came from working-class and poor families. Middle-class young men often received college deferments or found places in the National Guard at home. In 1965 the number of young men drafted each month doubled, and the draft made the war a direct concern for millions of families.

stem: The pattern described in the passage best supports which conclusion about the burden of the war?

options.text: Fighting fell mostly on working-class and poor men, while better-off men avoided service
The draft took young men from every class in exactly equal numbers
options.misconception: The passage says 80 percent came from working-class and poor families, so the burden was not equal.

options.text: College deferments were given only to young men from poor families
options.misconception: Background: college deferments went to young men in college, who were more often middle class, not poor.

options.text: The war touched only the families of men who volunteered to fight
options.misconception: The draft made the war a concern for millions of families, including families of draftees, not only volunteers.

rationales.A: Background: about 80 percent of the troops came from working-class and poor families, while middle-class men often gained deferments or Guard places.
rationales.B: The passage says about 80 percent of the troops came from working-class and poor families, so the burden was not equal.
rationales.C: Background: college deferments went to young men in college, who were more often middle class, not poor.
rationales.D: The passage says the draft made the war a direct concern for millions of families, not only for volunteers' families.
rationales.general:
1. The passage gives a share first: about 80 percent of the troops came from working-class and poor families.
2. It then gives the other side: middle-class young men often received college deferments or Guard places at home.
3. Background: in 1965 the monthly draft calls doubled, so the burden grew just as its unfairness became visible.
4. The war was therefore fought mostly by those with the fewest ways out of it.
Remember: When one group supplies most of the soldiers, ask who found a way out.
